'''''Bowiea''''', commonly known as '''climbing-onion''', is a genus of extremely poisonous, bulbous, perennial, succulent plants which thrive in dry and desert regions of eastern and southern [[Africa]], ranging from [[Uganda]] to [[South Africa]].<ref name=POWO>{{cite taxon |POWO |id=531999-1 |title=''Bowiea volubilis'' Harv. ex T.Moore & Mast. |access-date=February 5, 2026}}</ref><ref name=COL>{{Catalogue of Life |id=CCTQ9 |title=''Bowiea volubilis'' Harv. ex T.Moore & Mast. |access-date=February 5, 2026}}</ref> It is native to a region stretching from [[Kenya]] to [[Cape Province]].<ref name="ugubuugu">[http://apps.kew.org/wcsp/namedetail.do?name_id=300993 Kew World Checklist of Selected Plant Families]</ref> It is the 14th most commonly sold [[Medicinal plants|medicinal plant]] in South Africa, used to treat various health conditions. Due to massive harvesting, populations of this plant have been significantly reduced.<ref name=":1">{{Cite book |last=Van Jaarsveld |first=E. |title=Illustrated Handbook of Succulent Plants: Monocotyledons |publisher=Springer |year=2012 |isbn=978-3-642-56715-5 |pages=276–278 |chapter=Bowiea}}</ref> Due to its unique appearance, it is sometimes cultivated as a houseplant.<ref name=":3">{{Cite book |last=Zachos |first=Ellen |title=Growing healthy houseplants: choose the right plant, water wisely, and control pests |date=2014 |publisher=Storey Publishing |isbn=978-1-61212-440-7 |series=Storey basics |location=North Adams, MA |pages=86–87}}</ref>

The genus contains a single species, '''''Bowiea volubilis''''', named after the nineteenth-century British plant collector at [[Kew]], [[James Bowie (botanist)|James Bowie]].<ref>Govaerts, R. (1996). World Checklist of Seed Plants 2(1, 2): 1-492. Continental Publishing, Deurne.</ref><ref>Stedje, B. (1996). Hyacinthaceae. Flora of Tropical East Africa: 1-32.</ref> The specific epithet means ''twisting'' or ''winding'' in [[Latin]].<ref>{{Cite book |last=Gledhill |first=David |title=The names of plants |publisher=Cambridge University Press |year=2008 |isbn=978-0-511-47376-0 |edition=4}}</ref>

== Geographical range ==
Within the species, two [[subspecies]] with distinct geographical ranges have been identified. The subspecies ''Bowiea'' subsp. ''volubilis'' is found in the area stretching from tropical [[East Africa]] ([[Kenya]], [[Tanzania]], and [[Uganda]]) to [[Mozambique]], [[Zimbabwe]], [[Malawi]], [[Angola]], and the southeastern part of [[South Africa]]. In South Africa, it occurs in the [[Eastern Cape Province]], [[KwaZulu-Natal]], [[Mpumalanga]], [[Gauteng]], and [[Limpopo]].<ref name=":1" />

The subspecies ''B.'' subsp. ''gariepensis'' is found in southern [[Namibia]] and in the western part of the [[Northern Cape Province]] in South Africa, primarily in the eastern portion of the rocky Gariep Desert.<ref name=":1" />

== Description ==
[[File:Bowiea volubilis 122173532.jpg|left|thumb|Habit]]

=== Habit ===
[[Perennial]], [[Herbaceous plant|herbaceous]] [[Vine|climbing plants]].<ref name=":1" />
[[File:Bowiea volubilis 005.jpg|left|thumb|Bulb]]

=== Stem ===
The plants have many overlapping [[succulent]] scales, which form a tight, pale green, spherical [[bulb]] that grows to {{cvt|20|cm}} above the soil, sending up a twining fresh-green branched stem up to {{cvt|4.5|m}} in length, resembling green spaghetti,<ref>{{cite book | last= Hogan | first= Sean | date= 2004 |title= Flora - The Gardener's Bible | location= Willoughby, New South Wales | publisher= Global Book Pub. Pty. Ltd. | page= 248 | isbn= 1-74048-097-X }}</ref> with few linear deciduous leaves. The bulbs have a [[Sympodial branching|sympodial]] structure, and the terminal bud, forming both daughter bulbs and flower stem primordia, is located at the base of the innermost storage leaf. There are few [[stoma]]ta on the outer surface of the storage leaves, and their volume consists of a large-celled [[ground tissue]], storing water. Dormant in winter, when the outer scales and many of the scale tips dry to a paper-like state, the plants burst to growth in late spring or summer, producing one or more very fast-growing stems that needs to be supported by a trellis or stake. The stems are covered with many leafless side-branches that may fall off. The small greenish-white flowers appear in spring.<ref name=":1" />

=== Leaves ===
Short-lived, fleshy, lanceolate-linear, channelled leaves are only formed by young, immature individuals.<ref name=":1" />[[File:Bowiea volubilis kz04.jpg|thumb|left|Flower of ''B.'' subsp. ''volubilis'']]
[[File:嘉麗仙鞭草 Bowiea gariepensis - panoramio.jpg|left|thumb|Flower of ''B.'' subsp. ''gariepensis'']]

=== Flowers ===
The annual, [[Photosynthesis|photosynthetic]], climbing flower stem is twisted or spreading, highly branched, with needle-like branches up to 7 cm long, slightly fleshy, blue to blue-green in the subspecies ''gariepensis'', reaching up to 1.2 m in length, and green in the subspecies ''volubilis'', up to 10 m long (usually 3–4 m,<ref name=":1" /> and typically up to 2 m in container-grown plants).<ref name=":4">{{Cite book |title=Rośliny pokojowe: praktyczna encyklopedia |publisher=Hachette Livre Polska |year=2009 |isbn=978-83-7575-544-2 |editor-last=Mioulane |editor-first=Patrick |location=Warsaw |page=438 |language=pl |oclc=751318123}}</ref> The [[bract]]s are lanceolate and pointed.<ref name=":1" /> The [[Pedicel (botany)|pedicels]] are arching,<ref name=":1" /> measuring 2–5 cm in length.<ref name=POWO/> The [[inflorescence]] is described as a branched [[raceme]] with unisexual flowers in the lower section.<ref name=":5">{{Cite book |last1=Manning |first1=John |title=The color encyclopedia of cape bulbs |last2=Goldblatt |first2=Peter |last3=Snijman |first3=D. A. |date=2002 |publisher=Timber Press |isbn=978-0-88192-547-0 |location=Portland |pages=95–96}}</ref> The flowers have an unpleasant odor and are long-lasting.<ref name=":1" /> The [[perianth]] is radial,<ref name=":5" /> six-lobed, white (''B.'' subsp. ''gariepensis'') or green to yellowish-green (''B.'' subsp. ''volubilis'').<ref name=":1" /> The perianth segments are equal, free, lanceolate to oblong, with edges turned and unwound outward towards the base and slightly pointed tips, spreading to recurved, measuring 12 mm in length and 3.5 mm in width.<ref name=":1" /> There are six almost erect [[stamen]]s,<ref name=":1" /> with narrowly triangular to filiform filaments, and oblong heads.<ref name=POWO/> The [[Ovary (botany)|ovary]] is sessile,<ref name=POWO/> semi-inferior,<ref name=":6">{{Cite book |last=Speta |first=F. |url=http://link.springer.com/10.1007/978-3-662-03533-7 |title=Flowering Plants · Monocotyledons |publisher=Springer Berlin Heidelberg |year=1998 |isbn=978-3-642-08377-8 |editor-last=Kubitzki |editor-first=Klaus |volume=3 |location=Berlin, Heidelberg |page=272 |language= |chapter=Hyacinthaceae |doi=10.1007/978-3-662-03533-7}}</ref> three-chambered, broad-conical, light green, sticky in the upper part,<ref name=":1" /> containing about 5 ovules in each chamber.<ref name=":6" /> The carpel is syncarpous,<ref name=":6" /> with a short, round stigma, ending in a three-branched stigma.<ref name=":1" />

=== Fruits ===
Three-chambered, erect [[Capsule (fruit)|capsules]], measuring 9–25 mm in size,<ref name=POWO/> spherical and flattened with notched valves (subsp. ''gariepensis'') or cone-shaped with pointed valves (subsp. ''volubilis''),<ref name=":1" /> papery,<ref name=":6" /> splitting longitudinally, with remnants of perianth segments at the base,<ref name=":6" /> containing black, shiny, angular, oblong<ref name=":1" /> and flattened [[seed]]s up to 10 mm in length.<ref name=POWO/>

=== Similar species ===
Species of the genus ''[[Drimia]]'', classified in the section ''Schizobasis'' (formerly classified as a separate genus), which have upright (non-climbing), non-fleshy flower stems and short-lived flowers with an upper ovary, slightly fused at the base perianth segments, which fall off before fruiting.<ref name=":1" /> These plants were previously considered related, but their similarity results from [[convergent evolution]].<ref name=":5" />

== Biology and ecology ==

=== Habitat and development ===
''Bowiea'' subsp. ''volubilis'' occurs at low to medium altitudes, usually along mountain ranges, in densely vegetated river valleys, under clumps of bushes, and on boulders. The species has also been recorded on the edges of the [[Karoo]] and in bushy ravines (''kloof''). This subspecies also occurs in open forests or on steep rocky hillsides, usually in well-shaded areas. It tolerates both wet and dry conditions, mainly growing in areas with summer rainfall, with annual precipitation ranging from 200 to 800 mm.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |last=Parbhoo |first=Suvarna |title=PlantZAfrica: Bowiea volubilis |url=http://pza.sanbi.org/bowiea-volubilis |access-date=2024-04-26 |website=South African National Biodiversity Institute}}</ref> It blooms in spring and summer.<ref name=":1" /> Individual specimens live for about 10 years (at least under cultivation).<ref name=":4" />

''B''. subsp. ''gariepensis'' inhabits cooler [[scree]]s in the [[Orange River]] valley. It blooms in autumn and winter.<ref name=":1" />

The flowers of these plants, with a scent considered unpleasant, are pollinated by [[Fly|flies]] from the families ''[[Tachinidae]]'' and ''[[Muscidae]]'', as well as ''[[Vespidae]]''.<ref name=":5" />

After fruiting, the aboveground parts of both subspecies die off, and the plants enter a period of dormancy.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Asakawa |first=Sharon |title=Planting designs for cactus & succulents. Indoor & outdoor projects for unique, easy-care plants-in all climates |date=15 January 2014 |publisher=Cool Springs Press |isbn=978-1-59186-561-2 |location=Minneapolis |page=55}}</ref>

=== Phytochemical characteristics ===
The plant is highly poisonous.<ref name=":7">{{Cite book |last=Quattrocchi |first=Umberto |title=CRC world dictionary of medicinal and poisonous plants: common names, scientific names, eponyms, synonyms, and etymology |date=2012 |publisher=CRC press |isbn=978-1-4398-9442-2 |location=Boca Raton |page=640 |oclc=774639599}}</ref> All parts of ''Bowiea'' contain several active [[cardiac glycoside]]s, including bufadienolide glycosides.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Masondo |first1=N.A. |last2=Ndhlala |first2=A.R. |last3=Aremu |first3=A.O. |last4=Van Staden |first4=J. |last5=Finnie |first5=J.F. |year=2013 |title=A comparison of the pharmacological properties of garden cultivated and muthi market-sold Bowiea volubilis |journal=South African Journal of Botany |language= |volume=86 |pages=135–138 |doi=10.1016/j.sajb.2013.02.169|bibcode=2013SAJB...86..135M |doi-access=free }}</ref> The bulbs of this plant also contain compounds such as boworuboside, bowocryptoside, hellebrigenin, and various [[polysaccharide]]s.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Duke |first=James A. |title=Handbook of phytochemical constituents of GRAS herbs and other economic plants |date=2001 |publisher=CRC Press |isbn=978-0-8493-3865-6 |series=Herbal reference library series |location=Boca Raton, FL |pages=98–99}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Buckingham |first=John |title=Dictionary of Natural Products, Supplement 1 |date=25 November 2020 |publisher=CRC Press LLC |isbn=9781000109986 |location=Milton |page=38}}</ref>

=== Genetics ===
The [[chromosome]] number ([[Diploid|2n]]) of both subspecies is 20. The chromosomal complement consists of two pairs of large (LSt), two pairs of medium-sized (MSt), and three pairs of small (SSt) subacrocentric chromosomes, as well as three pairs of small submetacentric chromosomes (SSm).<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Bruyns |first1=Peter V. |last2=Vosa |first2=Canio G. |year=1987 |title=Taxonomic and Cytological Notes on Bowiea Hook. F. and Allied Genera (Liliaceae) |journal=Caryologia |language= |volume=40 |issue=4 |pages=287–297 |doi=10.1080/00087114.1987.10797831 |issn=0008-7114|doi-access=free }}</ref>

==Species==

=== Taxonomic position ===
The species belongs to the [[Monotypic taxon|monotypic genus]] ''Bowiea'', which in classification systems of the second decade of the 21st century (including the APG IV system) is placed in the tribe ''Urgineeae'', subfamily ''[[Scilloideae]]'', within the family ''[[Asparagaceae]]''.<ref>{{Cite web |title=USDA, Agricultural Research Service, National Plant Germplasm System. 2020. Germplasm Resources Information Network (GRIN-Taxonomy) |url=https://npgsweb.ars-grin.gov/gringlobal/taxon/taxonomysearch |access-date=2024-04-26 |website=npgsweb.ars-grin.gov}}</ref> The genus is [[Sister group|sister]] to the genus ''[[Drimia]]''.<ref name=":1" />

Historically, the genus was classified in the family ''[[Hyacinthaceae]]''. In the [[Takhtajan system]] from 1997, the genus ''Bowiea'' was classified, together with the genus ''Schizobasis'' (now included in the genus ''Drimia''), in the tribe ''Bowieae'' <small>Hutch</small>. in the family ''Hyacinthaceae'' in the order ''[[Amaryllidales]]''.<ref>{{Cite web |year=1989 |editor-last=Brands |editor-first=S. J. |title=The Taxonomicon |url=http://taxonomicon.taxonomy.nl/ |access-date=2024-04-26 |website=taxonomicon.taxonomy.nl}}</ref> In the Takhtajan system from 2009, the author classified the genus in the subfamily ''Urgineoideae'' within the family ''Hyacinthaceae''.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Takhtaja︡n |first=Armen |title=Flowering plants |publisher=Springer |year=2009 |isbn=978-1-4020-9608-2 |edition=2 |location=New York |page=668}}</ref> In the [[Reveal system]] from 2007, the genus was classified in the subtribe ''Bowieinae'' within the tribe ''Bowieae'' in the family ''Hyacinthaceae''.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Reveal |first=James L. |date=2007-10-01 |title=Indices Nominum Supragenericorum Plantarum Vascularium |url=http://www.plantsystematics.org/reveal/pbio/fam/inspv2.html |access-date=2024-04-26 |website=www.plantsystematics.org}}</ref>

=== Species division ===
One species is recognized, with two subspecies<ref name="ugubuugu"/>

*''Bowiea volubilis'' (climbing-onion, sea onion<ref>{{cite web |title=Top 10 ugly plants |website=[[The Daily Telegraph]] |date=12 June 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220821211329/https://www.telegraph.co.uk/gardening/gardeningpicturegalleries/5506103/Top-10-ugly-plants.html?image=8 |archive-date=2022-08-21 |url-status=live |url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/gardening/gardeningpicturegalleries/5506103/Top-10-ugly-plants.html?image=8}}</ref>)
**''Bowiea volubilis'' subsp. ''gariepensis'' <small>(van Jaarsv.) Bruyns</small> – Namibia, Cape Province
**''Bowiea volubilis'' subsp. ''volubilis'' – from Cape Province to Kenya

=== Nomenclatural type ===
The [[holotype]] of ''Bowiea'' subsp. ''gariepensis'', collected in 1982 on Groot Pellaberg mountain near the town of [[Pofadder, South Africa|Pofadder]] in South Africa, is stored in the [[herbarium]] of [[Kirstenbosch National Botanical Garden]] in [[Cape Town]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Holotype of Bowiea volubilis Harv. ex Hook.f. subsp. gariepensis (Van Jaarsv.) Bruyns [family HYACINTHACEAE] on JSTOR |url=https://plants.jstor.org/stable/10.5555/al.ap.specimen.nbg0127051-1 |access-date=2024-04-26 |website=plants.jstor.org |doi=}}</ref>

== Threats and preservation ==
The subspecies ''Bowiea volubilis'' has been listed on the Red List of South African Plants as [[vulnerable species]]. This plant is under significant pressure due to harvesting for medicinal purposes across most of its range. Between 1977 and 2007, the population decline of this subspecies in South Africa exceeded 30%. Over the past 10 years, a 40% decline has been recorded in the monitored subpopulation in one of the private nature reserves, and another known subpopulation has been completely destroyed. In 2000, South African authorities confiscated 1,300 illegally collected bulbs of this plant.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Threatened Species Programme {{!}} SANBI Red List of South African Plants |url=http://redlist.sanbi.org/species.php?species=3811-3 |access-date=2024-04-26 |website=redlist.sanbi.org}}</ref>

''Bowiea'' subsp. ''gariepensis'' has been listed on the Red List of South African Plants with a status of [[Least-concern species|least concern]].<ref>{{Cite web |last1=van Jaarsveld |first1=E. J. |last2=Potter |first2=L. |year=2005 |title=National Assessment: Red List of South African Plants version 2020.1 |url=http://redlist.sanbi.org/species.php?species=3811-4 |access-date=2024-04-26 |website=redlist.sanbi.org}}</ref>

== Uses ==

=== Medicinal ===
Even though this plant is highly toxic, traditional healers in South Africa have long used ''Bowiea'' as a herbal remedy for various ailments, particularly for [[skin diseases]], [[eye irritation]],<ref name=":8">{{Cite journal |last1=Ramarumo |first1=Luambo Jeffrey |last2=Maroyi |first2=Allfred |last3=Tshisikhawe |first3=M. P. |year=2019 |title=Bowiea volubilis Harv. ex Hook.f. subsp. volubilis: A therapeutic plant species used by the traditional healers in the Soutpansberg Region, Vhembe Biosphere Reserve, Limpopo Province, South Africa |journal=Journal of Pharmaceutical Sciences and Research |volume=11 |issue=7 |pages=2538–2542}}</ref> [[palpitations]],<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Dauncey |first1=Elizabeth A. |title=Plants That Kill: A Natural History of the World's Most Poisonous Plants |last2=Larsson |first2=Sonny |publisher=Princeton University Press |year=2018 |isbn=978-0-691-17876-9 |page=61}}</ref> [[headache]]s, [[muscle pains]], [[infertility]], [[urinary tract infection]]s, and [[Sexually transmitted infection|sexually transmitted diseases]].<ref name=":9">{{Cite journal |last1=Aremu |first1=Adeyemi O. |last2=Moyo |first2=Mack |last3=Amoo |first3=Stephen O. |last4=Van Staden |first4=Johannes |year=2015 |title=Ethnobotany, therapeutic value, phytochemistry and conservation status of Bowiea volubilis: A widely used bulbous plant in southern Africa |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0378874115300763 |journal=Journal of Ethnopharmacology |language= |volume=174 |pages=308–316 |doi=10.1016/j.jep.2015.08.009|pmid=26277489 |url-access=subscription }}</ref> When combined with other plants, it is also used as an antiparasitic for infants, for [[hepatitis]], [[pelvic pain]] in women, and [[jaundice]] in children.<ref name=":8" /> The plant is also used to induce [[abortion]].<ref name=":10">{{Cite book |last=Bajaj |first=Y. P. S |title=Biotechnology in Agriculture and Forestry |publisher=Springer Verlag |year=2013 |isbn=978-3-662-30369-6 |series=Medicinal and Aromatic Plants VII |volume=28 |location=Berlin}}</ref> An [[enema]] of bulb infusion is used for [[impotence]].<ref name=":11">{{Cite book |last1=Dold |first1=Tony |title=Voices from the forest: celebrating nature and culture in Xhosaland |last2=Cocks |first2=Michelle |date=2012 |publisher=Jacana |isbn=978-1-4314-0299-1 |location=Auckland Park, South Africa |page=200}}</ref>

A [[decoction]] of the bulbs is used by the [[Xhosa people]] as a [[laxative]], while the [[Mfengu]] and [[Mpondo people|Mpondo]] use ground roasted bulbs for the same purpose. [[Zulu people]] use a water extract from the fresh outer scales as a remedy for [[ascites]], infertility, urinary tract infections, back pain, and muscle pains. [[Swazi people]] use a decoction of ''Bowiea'' and ''Boophane disticha'' bulbs for [[scabies]]. In traditional medicine in the Western Cape Province, the bulbs are applied topically for skin rashes, acne, cuts, burns, and insect bites. Bulbs are also used in KwaZulu-Natal to prepare mixtures to facilitate childbirth, treat headaches, and infertility.<ref name=":9" />

The [[cardiac glycoside]]s present in these plants have cardiotonic, laxative, irritant, emetic, anti-inflammatory, antibacterial, and antifungal properties.<ref name=":7" /> The effect of glycosides present in the bulbs is 30 times stronger than those of [[Digitalis|foxglove]] glycosides, and those present in the flowers are 60 times stronger.<ref name=":10" />

Due to the presence of cardiac glycosides, the entire plant is highly poisonous.<ref name=":7" /> Symptoms of overdose include vomiting, [[hypersalivation]], [[arrhythmia]], and spasms, which can lead to death within minutes or hours (depending on the dosage). Autopsies of individuals who died from poisoning by this plant showed irritation of the digestive system, congestion of the liver and other internal organs, and cardiac arrest during the [[Diastole|diastolic]] phase.<ref name=":10" />

=== Ornamental ===
Due to its unusual appearance, ''Bowiea'' is cultivated as an ornamental plant, especially as a houseplant<ref name=":3" /> (referred to as "extraordinary"<ref name=":12">{{Cite book |last=Sarwa |first=Andrzej Juliusz |title=Mała encyklopedia doniczkowych roślin ozdobnych |publisher=Karat |year=1994 |isbn=83-85601-39-2 |location=Tarnów |language=pl |oclc=749516926}}</ref> and "a true curiosity").<ref name=":13">{{Cite book |last1=Schubert |first1=Margot |title=Mieszkamy wśród kwiatów |last2=Herwig |first2=Rob |publisher=Państwowe Wydawnictwo Rolnicze i Leśne |year=1984 |isbn=83-09-00563-6 |location=Warsaw |page=146 |language=pl |oclc=749830845}}</ref>

=== Magical ===
In Africa, this plant is regarded as having magical properties. It is believed that it makes warriors brave and invincible, protects travelers, and enables the release of love.<ref name=":2" /> ''Bowiea'' is also believed to repel bandits and protect homes from lightning and hail.<ref name=":10" /> A decoction of the bulbs is taken orally as a remedy for ''idliso'' caused by witchcraft.<ref name=":11" />

==Cultivation==
The plant is described as very easy to grow.<ref name=":3" />

=== Requirements ===
The soil should be porous and well-draining<ref name=":14">{{Cite book |title=American Horticultural Society encyclopedia of plants & flowers |date=2011 |publisher=DK Pub |isbn=978-0-7566-6857-0 |editor-last=Brickell |editor-first=Christopher |location=London; New York |page=523 |editor-last2=American Horticultural Society}}</ref> – it's recommended to use standard [[cactus]] soil,<ref name=":4" /> according to some authors, in weathered clay.<ref name=":13" /><ref name=":12" /> The container should be wide and rather shallow.<ref name=":13" /><ref name=":12" /> Plants should be repotted every two years, in spring,<ref name=":4" /> or as needed (e.g., when there are many offsets).<ref name=":12" /> The location should be bright,<ref name=":4" /> sunny<ref name=":14" /> (it won't bloom in areas without direct sunlight).<ref name=":3" /> It requires regular but moderate watering during the growing season<ref name=":14" /> (some sources specify that watering every 10 days is sufficient).<ref name=":4" /> Bulbs should not be soaked as their coverings easily rot.<ref name=":4" /> Fertilization according to different authors is recommended once or twice a season<ref name=":4" /> or once a month.<ref name=":12" /> The plant needs support as the flower stalks do not form [[tendril]]s.<ref name=":14" /> In natural conditions, plants go through a dormant period once a year, during which the flower stalk dies. In indoor conditions, the plant can remain evergreen, but if it enters a dormant period (which happens in summer),<ref name=":12" /><ref name=":13" /> watering should be reduced to once a week until a new shoot appears<ref name=":3" /> (according to other sources, watering and fertilizing should be completely suspended during this time).<ref name=":4" /><ref name=":12" /><ref name=":13" /> Some authors recommend moving the bulb into a cool place during dormancy – at a temperature of about 10 °C<ref name=":12" /> or even slightly lower.<ref name=":13" />

=== Propagation ===
Plants are propagated from seeds, offsets (often numerous in cultivation next to the parent bulb),<ref name=":13" /> or by rooting cuttings of the bulb's storage leaves, which produce offsets on the cut surface.<ref name=":1" />

=== Pests ===
They are usually not present,<ref name=":12" /> but [[mealybug]]s, [[Diaspididae|armored scale insects]], and various [[aphids]] can appear.<ref name=":4" />
